explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. David says, "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want" (Psalm 23:1). The word "want" there means to lack or go without. When the Good Shepherd leads, the sheep has everything it needs. It's like a cookie box that never runs empty.

Not quite, friend. David isn't saying he has to earn his keep. He says, "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want" (Psalm 23:1). A sheep doesn't earn the grass it lies in. The shepherd just provides it. No invoice at the pasture gate.

Close, but not the word, baker. David says he will not lack what he needs because "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want" (Psalm 23:1). It's about not lacking, not about not losing things. The difference matters. The shepherd keeps him full, not just keeps him from losing.

Exactly, baker. Green pastures and quiet waters paint a picture of rest and peace. David says, "He makes me lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside quiet waters" (Psalm 23:2). No rushing, no noise. Just the shepherd settling his sheep where they can breathe easy. Like finally kicking off your shoes after a long day.

Not this time, friend. Pastures and still waters aren't about hustle. David says, "He makes me lie down in green pastures" (Psalm 23:2). Lying down is the opposite of hustle. You know that feeling when your phone finally stops buzzing and you can just sit? That's the vibe. Total quiet.

Nope, baker. Green pastures and quiet waters are safe places. The psalm says, "He makes me lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside quiet waters" (Psalm 23:2). That's a picture of peace, not danger. The scary valley comes later in the song, not here.

That's the word, baker. David says, "He restores my soul" (Psalm 23:3). Restore means to bring back to health, to renew. When your soul is worn thin, the LORD patches it up. It's like a stamper with worn edges getting sharpened again.

Not tests, friend. David says, "He restores my soul" (Psalm 23:3). The LORD doesn't test the soul to break it. He restores it. The word means renewing, bringing back to life, not putting under pressure.
Weighs isn't it, baker. The verse says, "He restores my soul" (Psalm 23:3). Weighing would be measuring on a scale, but restoring is healing. David's soul gets refreshed and renewed, not measured.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His name
explanations.explanation: Right you are, baker. David says the LORD guides him "in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name" (Psalm 23:3). The shepherd's reputation is on the line. His name is His glory, and He leads His sheep in ways that honor Him. Like a baker whose name is on every box.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His flock
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. It's not for the flock's sake. David says the LORD guides him "for the sake of His name" (Psalm 23:3). The sheep benefits, sure, but the reason given is the LORD's own name and glory. He acts to protect who He is.

explanations.answer: For the sake of His land
explanations.explanation: No, baker. Not the land. The verse says, "for the sake of His name" (Psalm 23:3). It's about the LORD's name, His reputation. He leads David in right paths because of His own character, not because of the territory.

explanations.answer: Because the LORD is with him
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. David says, "I will fear no evil, for You are with me" (Psalm 23:4). The reason there's no fear in the dark valley is the shepherd's presence. He's not alone down there. The LORD walks right beside him, step for step.

Not alone, friend. David says, "I will fear no evil, for You are with me" (Psalm 23:4). It's not about David's own strength. It's about the LORD being there with him. No sheep is strong enough to walk that valley alone.

Nope, baker. David doesn't say the valley is short. He says, "I will fear no evil, for You are with me" (Psalm 23:4). The reason is the LORD's presence, not the length of the walk. Even a long valley is safe with the shepherd beside you.

True, baker. David says, "Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me" (Psalm 23:4). In the valley of the shadow of death, the shepherd's tools bring comfort. They protect and guide. They're a sign the shepherd is still on the job.

Actually it's true, friend. The text says, "Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me" (Psalm 23:4). David feels comforted by them even in the dark valley. The rod and staff mean the shepherd is defending him, not hurting him.

Table is right, baker. David says, "You prepare a table before me" (Psalm 23:5). Not a tent, not a bed. A table means a meal, a feast. The LORD is the host and David is the honored guest. Like walking into a bakery and finding a fresh batch waiting just for you.

Not a tent, friend. David says, "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies" (Psalm 23:5). A tent is for sleeping under, but this is a table for eating. It's about being fed and honored, even with enemies watching.

Bed's not the word, baker. The verse says, "You prepare a table before me" (Psalm 23:5). A table is for a meal. David's picture changes from a sheep in a field to a guest at a feast. The host sets the table and fills the cups.

No, friend, that's not what the text says. David says the LORD prepares his table "in the presence of my enemies" (Psalm 23:5). Not far away from them. "In the presence" means right there where they can see it. The point is the LORD's protection is public and bold.

False is right, baker. The text says the LORD prepares the table "in the presence of my enemies" (Psalm 23:5). Not far away from them. Right in front of them. That's the bold part of the verse. The shepherd doesn't hide David; He honors him publicly.

Exactly, baker. David says, "my cup overflows" (Psalm 23:5). An overflowing cup means more than enough. The shepherd doesn't just give David what he needs; He gives him abundance. The cup runs over like a mixing bowl that's too full.

Not careless, friend. "My cup overflows" means abundance, not carelessness (Psalm 23:5). When a cup overflows, it's full to the brim and spilling over. David has more than he can hold, not less than he needs.

No rushing here, baker. An overflowing cup means plenty, not hurry. David says, "my cup overflows" (Psalm 23:5). It's a picture of blessing poured out until it spills over. Nothing about being rushed or hurried.

Right, baker. David says, "Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life" (Psalm 23:6). Goodness and mercy are the two things chasing after him. They follow like loyal dogs at his heels. All his days, not just the good ones.

Not wealth and honor, friend. The verse says, "Surely goodness and mercy will follow me" (Psalm 23:6). David isn't talking about money or fame. He's talking about the LORD's goodness and covenant love pursuing him every single day.

No, baker. Not strength and wisdom. David says, "goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life" (Psalm 23:6). Those are the two things that pursue him. Personal power isn't what follows; it's the shepherd's character chasing him down.

explanations.answer: In the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the close, baker. David says, "I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever" (Psalm 23:6). The house of the LORD is His presence. Forever means no end date, no closing time. David ends his song looking home to the only place that never runs out.

Not Hebron, friend. David says, "I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever" (Psalm 23:6). Hebron was a real city where David ruled, but that's not where he says he'll dwell forever. It's the LORD's house, not an earthly city.

Not Canaan, baker. The verse says, "I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever" (Psalm 23:6). Canaan was the promised land, but David's final picture is the LORD's own house. That's where he wants to be forever, not just in the land.
